topics.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
topics.summary: Turn vague scale into QPS, storage and bandwidth in two minutes, and let the numbers pick the design.

blocks.text: Estimation exists to justify design decisions: do we need a cache, sharding, a CDN, a queue? Estimate only what changes the design, round aggressively, and say the conclusion out loud.

head: Operation
Approx. time
rows: Round trip in one data center

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Memory is ~100× faster than SSD, SSD ~100× faster than a cross-continent round trip. That ladder is why caches and CDNs exist.
500M daily active users, each reads 20 items and writes 1 item (1 KB) per day.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Read-heavy at 20:1, so I'll put a cache in front of the database. 5k writes/s fits a sharded store. 180 TB a year means partitioning from day one.
Serial dependencies multiply (99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%). Parallel redundancy adds nines: two independent 99% replicas ≈ 99.99%.

items: Pin the user count: DAU and how many actions each does per day.
Convert to QPS: actions/day ÷ 10^5. Multiply by 2–3 for peak (10× for flash sales, ticket drops, match finishes).
Split read vs write QPS; state the ratio — it decides cache-heavy vs write-heavy designs.
Storage: writes/day × object size × retention days × replication (3). Add indexes (~30%).
Bandwidth: QPS × response size (ingress for writes, egress for reads).
Memory for cache: hot fraction (often 20%) × daily read set × object size.
Servers: peak QPS ÷ per-node capacity, then +30–50% headroom and N+1 per AZ.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Write the numbers in a corner of the board and point back to them when you justify a cache, a shard count or a CDN.

**Concurrency = throughput × latency.** 10k req/s at 200 ms means 2,000 requests in flight; with 200 threads per server you need 10 servers just to hold them. Use it to size thread pools, connection pools and WebSocket fleets.

DB pool size ≈ queries/s × avg query time
  5,000 q/s × 4 ms = 20 connections busy on average → pool of ~40 with headroom

items.q: How many servers for 1M concurrent WebSocket users?
items.a: At ~50k connections per server with headroom → ~25–30 servers, spread across AZs, plus capacity to absorb one AZ failing (≈ +50%).

items.q: Why multiply storage by 3?
items.a: Typical replication factor for durability; erasure coding would be ~1.4–1.5× instead.

items.q: How precise should estimates be?
items.a: Order of magnitude. State assumptions, round to powers of ten, and move on in under 5 minutes.

items: **Reverse proxy**: sits in front of servers; TLS, compression, caching (NGINX).
**Load balancer**: a reverse proxy that spreads load across replicas.
**API gateway**: L7 proxy plus auth, rate limiting, API keys, request shaping, routing to microservices (Kong, AWS API Gateway).

Distributed scheduler with leader election / locks

items: **L4** works on TCP/UDP flows: NAT or direct server return; it can't see URLs; very fast (AWS NLB, Maglev, IPVS).
**L7** terminates TLS, parses HTTP, routes on path/host/header, retries, injects headers, does canaries (ALB, Envoy, NGINX).
**Global load balancing:** DNS (GeoDNS, latency-based), anycast IPs (Cloudflare, Google), or a global L7 front door.
**Maglev / consistent hashing** keeps a connection on the same backend even as LB instances change.
**Health checks:** active probes + passive outlier detection; slow-start new instances; drain on shutdown.
**Connection reuse:** keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing between LB and backends cut handshake cost.

How

Needs shared state across LB nodes
Pick 2 at random, choose the less loaded

items: Reactive (target tracking on CPU, RPS, queue depth) vs scheduled (known peaks) vs predictive (forecast).
Scale on a leading metric: queue depth or in-flight requests react faster than CPU.
Cold starts: JVM warmup and cache warming make new instances slow; pre-scale before events.
Keep N+1 per AZ so losing an AZ doesn't overload the rest (run at ≤ 66% across 3 AZs).
Protect downstreams: scaling the API 10× can melt the database; add connection pooling (PgBouncer) and limits.

head: Pattern
How
Trade-off
rows: One region serves, other on standby
Simple; failover takes minutes; idle cost
All regions read, writes to home region
Fast reads; write latency for far users
Limits blast radius; cross-cell features harder

items.q: L4 or L7 for WebSockets?
items.a: Either works: L4 passes the long-lived TCP through cheaply; L7 can route the upgrade by path and do auth. Use least-connections or consistent hashing.

items.q: How do you deploy without dropping requests?
items.a: Rolling or blue/green: mark instance unhealthy, drain in-flight requests (connection draining), then stop; readiness probes gate new instances.

items.q: What's a thundering herd at the LB?
items.a: Many clients reconnect at once after an outage; mitigate with jittered client backoff, admission control and slow start.

items.q: Sticky sessions — good or bad?
items.a: Avoid for HTTP (uneven load, failover loses state); acceptable for WebSockets or local cache affinity via consistent hashing.

How
Use for

You upload to the CDN ahead of time

**TTL** through Cache-Control (max-age, s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate).
**Versioned file names** (app.3f9c.js) so you never purge static assets.
**Purge API** for content that must change now; an origin shield stops a purge from stampeding the origin.
**Signed URLs / cookies** for private content (paid video).

head: Header / directive
Meaning
rows: Browser and shared caches may reuse for N seconds
Serve stale while fetching fresh in background
Separate cache entries per header value

items: Edge PoPs near users → regional / shield tier → origin. Each miss climbs one level.
Origin shield collapses many edge misses into one origin request (request coalescing).
Tiered caching lifts hit ratio for the long tail.
Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) for auth checks, A/B, header rewrites, personalization at the edge.

blocks.caption: Hit ratio improves at each tier

items: Segment video into 2–6 s chunks (HLS/DASH) so each segment caches independently.
Range requests for large files; CDN caches byte ranges or full objects.
Pre-warm (push) popular new content before a launch.
ISP-embedded caches (Netflix Open Connect, Google Global Cache) for very high egress.
TLS termination and certificate management at the edge.
DDoS absorption (anycast spreads attack traffic), WAF rules, bot management.
Signed URLs / cookies with expiry for paid or private content.
Origin only accepts traffic from the CDN (IP allowlist or auth header).

items.q: A deploy shipped broken CSS cached for a day. Fix?
items.a: Versioned asset names so new HTML points to new files; for the bad URL, purge it; set long TTL only on hashed assets.

items.q: Can you cache API responses at the CDN?
items.a: Yes for public, shared responses with short TTLs and correct cache keys; never personalized data under a shared key.

items.q: How do you measure CDN effectiveness?
items.a: Cache hit ratio (requests and bytes), origin offload, edge latency p95, error rate by PoP.

topics.title: Networking Essentials
topics.summary: What actually happens between client and server: DNS, TCP vs UDP, TLS, HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3, and L4 vs L7 load balancing — the vocabulary every design answer leans on.

head: Layer
What it does
Interview relevance
rows: Name → IP; TTL-cached at many levels
GeoDNS for routing users to regions; slow failover because of TTLs
Extra round trips (1-RTT in TLS 1.3); terminate at the LB
Versions differ in multiplexing and transport

cols.title: HTTP/1.1
cons: One request at a time per connection → browsers open ~6 connections

cols.title: HTTP/2
pros: Multiplexed streams over one TCP connection
cons: TCP head-of-line blocking: one lost packet stalls all streams

cols.title: HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP)
pros: Independent streams — no TCP HOL blocking

cols.title: L7 (HTTP)
pros: Route by path, header, cookie; TLS termination; retries

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd put an L7 load balancer in front of stateless HTTP services and an L4 balancer in front of the WebSocket gateways.

items: New HTTPS connection over TCP + TLS 1.3 ≈ DNS + 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) before the first byte of the request.
Cross-continent RTT ≈ 100–150 ms, so connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2) and edge termination (CDN) matter more than server speed.
Anycast IPs route users to the nearest edge PoP.

items.q: Why does DNS failover take minutes?
items.a: Resolvers and clients cache records for the TTL; lowering TTLs helps but increases DNS load.

items.q: Where do you terminate TLS?
items.a: At the edge / load balancer, re-encrypting to backends if the internal network isn't trusted (mTLS in a mesh).

items.q: Why do gRPC services need special load balancing?
items.a: HTTP/2 keeps one long-lived connection, so L4 balancing pins all requests to one backend; use L7 (per-request) or client-side balancing.

topics.title: Caching Strategies
topics.summary: Cache-aside by default; pick write strategy, eviction and invalidation deliberately and defend against stampedes.

blocks.caption: Closer to the user = faster, harder to invalidate

head: Strategy
How
Strength
Weakness
rows: App reads cache → on miss reads DB, fills cache; on write updates DB then deletes key
Cache library loads from DB on miss
Write cache, flush DB async in batches

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Delete the key on write instead of updating it: two concurrent updates can leave the older value in the cache. For tighter freshness, invalidate from the DB change stream (CDC).

head: Policy
Evicts
Good for
rows: General default (hash map + doubly linked list, O(1))

head: Problem
What happens
Fix
rows: Hot key expires; thousands hit the DB at once
Single-flight / per-key lock, early probabilistic refresh, serve stale while revalidating
Lookups for keys that don't exist always miss
Cache nulls with short TTL; Bloom filter
Many keys expire together or cache dies
Jittered TTLs, multi-level cache, circuit breaker

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Cache-aside with a 5-minute jittered TTL; writes delete the key. For hot keys I coalesce misses so only one request reaches the database.

items: **The race:** reader A misses, reads old value from DB; writer B updates DB and deletes key; A then writes the old value into cache. Stale until TTL.

Mitigations: short TTL as safety net; delayed double delete; versioned values (store version, reject older sets); lease tokens (Facebook memcache leases) so only the reader holding the lease can fill.
**CDC-driven invalidation:** DB binlog → Debezium → Kafka → invalidator deletes keys. Ordered by commit, survives app bugs.
**Write-through with versions** for read-your-writes; route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after their write.

blocks.text:
Lease pattern (memcache):
 GET k → miss → server returns lease token L
 reader loads from DB, SET k v L  → accepted only if L still valid
 a DELETE in between invalidates L → stale fill rejected

head: Technique
How
Best for
rows: One in-flight load per key per process; others wait
SET lock:k NX PX; losers wait or serve stale
Refresh early with probability rising near TTL

items: Hit ratio drives everything: at 95% hits, DB sees 5% of traffic; dropping to 90% doubles DB load.
Working-set analysis: measure key popularity (Zipfian); 20% of keys often serve 80%+ of reads.
Memory = hot keys × (key + value + ~50–100 B overhead per entry).
Watch eviction rate; rising evictions with steady traffic means the cache is too small.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Quote the DB load at your hit ratio: "At 98% hits, 100k reads/s becomes 2k/s on the database."

cols.title: In-process (Caffeine, Guava)
cons: Each instance has its own copy

blocks.text: Common answer: two-level cache — small local LRU with seconds of TTL in front of Redis; invalidate via pub/sub broadcast.

items: Cache objects (user:42), query results (feed:42:page1), computed aggregates (counts), rendered fragments, negative results.
Key design: namespace + version + id (`v3:user:42`); bumping the version invalidates everything at once.
Don't cache: rapidly changing data with strict correctness (balances), very large values, highly personalized low-reuse data.
Serialization: compact formats (protobuf, MessagePack) cut memory and network.

items.q: Write-through or cache-aside for a product catalog?
items.a: Cache-aside with TTL and delete-on-write; catalog is read-heavy and occasional staleness is acceptable.

items.q: How do you keep cache and DB consistent?
items.a: You can't make them atomic; bound staleness with TTL, invalidate on write (or via CDC), and use leases/versions to avoid stale fills.

items.q: Cache went down; DB is overwhelmed. What now?
items.a: Circuit-break to serve degraded responses, rate-limit, warm the cache gradually, use replicas; long-term run cache with replicas and multiple AZs.

items.q: How do you cache paginated feeds?
items.a: Cache the list of IDs per user (or per page key) and hydrate objects from an object cache; cursor pagination keeps keys stable.

topics.title: Redis Deep Dive
topics.summary: Single-threaded in-memory data structure server: cache, sessions, counters, leaderboards, locks, queues.

items: **RDB** snapshots: compact, fast restart, can lose minutes.
**AOF** append log: fsync every second loses ≤ 1 s; rewrite compacts it.
**Replication** is async: failover can lose the last writes.
**Sentinel** monitors and promotes a replica automatically.
**Cluster**: 16,384 hash slots, slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. Use hash tags `{user:42}` to keep related keys together for multi-key ops.
Atomic multi-step logic via **Lua scripts** or MULTI/EXEC.

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Redis is not your system of record unless you accept losing the last second of writes. Use it as a cache or for data you can rebuild.

Lock:         SET lock:job42 <uuid> NX PX 30000   (release via Lua compare-and-delete)
Rate limit:   INCR rl:u42:1730100000 ; EXPIRE 60
Leaderboard:  ZINCRBY lb 10 user42 ; ZREVRANGE lb 0 9 WITHSCORES
Session:      HSET sess:abc uid 42 ; EXPIRE sess:abc 1800
Delayed job:  ZADD jobs <runAtMillis> job42 ; ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs 0 <now>

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Redis executes commands on one thread, so INCR and SET NX are atomic without extra locking. For anything multi-step I'd use a Lua script.

items: Event loop (epoll/kqueue) on a single thread executes commands; since 6.0, I/O threads handle socket reads/writes.
Encodings: small hashes/sets/zsets use compact listpacks; they convert to hash tables / skip lists past thresholds — memory-efficient for small objects.
Sorted set = skip list (ordered ops) + hash table (member lookup).
Expiry: lazy (checked on access) + active sampling of expired keys each cycle.
Persistence via `fork()`: copy-on-write snapshot; big datasets can double memory briefly during RDB/AOF rewrite.
Pipelining batches commands to cut round trips; MULTI/EXEC queues commands executed atomically (no rollback).

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: `KEYS *`, `FLUSHALL`, `SMEMBERS` on a million-member set, or `DEL` of a huge key block the single thread for everyone. Use SCAN and UNLINK.

head: Policy
Evicts from
Use
rows: Queues, sessions, anything you can't lose silently
Mixed cache + persistent data (better: separate instances)

blocks.text: LRU/LFU are approximated by sampling `maxmemory-samples` keys, not a perfect global order.

head: Setup
Gives you
Limits
rows: Still one primary's memory and CPU
Multi-key ops only within a slot; no SELECT db
Ops handled; MemoryDB adds durable multi-AZ log

In Cluster, all keys must be in one slot (hash tags).
Redis 7 Functions persist server-side libraries.

items.q: Redis vs Memcached?
items.a: Redis: data structures, persistence, replication, Lua, streams. Memcached: simple multi-threaded KV cache, slightly simpler to scale for pure caching.

items.q: How do you find big or hot keys?
items.a: `redis-cli --bigkeys`, `--hotkeys` (with LFU), MEMORY USAGE, and client-side metrics.

items.q: Is MULTI/EXEC a transaction?
items.a: It's atomic execution without rollback; use WATCH for optimistic concurrency (abort if a watched key changed).

items.q: How would you implement a sliding-window rate limiter?
items.a: Sorted set per key with timestamps; Lua: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE old, ZCARD, ZADD if under limit, EXPIRE.

topics.title: Databases & Indexing
topics.summary: Choose the store from the access pattern; understand B-trees vs LSM trees and what each index costs.

head: Need
Pick
Watch out
rows: Massive writes, key access, time series
Model each query as a table
Secondary index, not source of truth

blocks.text: LSM write path: commit log + memtable → flush to immutable SSTable → background compaction. Bloom filters skip SSTables that can't hold the key.

items: **Composite index** (a, b, c) serves queries on a, (a, b), (a, b, c): the leftmost-prefix rule.
**Covering index** answers the query from the index alone, no table lookup.
**Partial index** indexes only rows matching a condition (status = 'OPEN').
Every index speeds reads and slows writes and uses storage.
Use EXPLAIN: a sequential scan on a big table means a missing index.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: The hot query is 'orders for a customer, newest first', so the index is (customer_id, created_at DESC).

items: **WAL (write-ahead log):** every change is appended and fsynced before commit; crash recovery replays it. Durability = WAL on disk.
**Buffer pool:** hot pages in memory; dirty pages flushed by checkpoints.
**MVCC:** each row version carries transaction IDs; readers see a snapshot, writers create new versions; vacuum (Postgres) / purge (InnoDB) cleans old versions.
**Clustered index (InnoDB):** rows stored in primary-key order — random UUID PKs cause page splits; prefer sequential/time-ordered IDs.
**Query planner:** chooses index vs scan from statistics; stale stats → bad plans (`ANALYZE`).
Composite index order: equality columns first, then range, then sort: `(tenant_id, status, created_at)`.
Covering index (`INCLUDE`) avoids heap lookups.
Selectivity matters: an index on a boolean rarely helps.
Every index adds write amplification and storage; drop unused ones.
**Query-first design:** list access patterns, then design one table (or partition) per pattern; duplicate data freely.
**Cassandra:** PRIMARY KEY ((partition key), clustering cols). Partition = unit of distribution; keep partitions < ~100 MB; bucket by time to avoid unbounded partitions: `((chat_id, month), ts)`.
**DynamoDB:** partition key + sort key; GSIs for alternate access; single-table design with overloaded keys (`PK=USER#42`, `SK=ORDER#2026-10-29`).
**MongoDB:** embed when data is read together and bounded; reference when unbounded or shared.
Hot partitions are the #1 NoSQL failure: spread writes with high-cardinality keys or write sharding.

sections.title: OLTP vs OLAP and the data pipeline

blocks.text: Typical flow: OLTP → CDC (Debezium) → Kafka → stream processor / batch ETL → warehouse + lake (Parquet on S3) → BI and ML.

items: Postgres uses a process per connection; thousands of app instances need PgBouncer/RDS Proxy in transaction mode.
N+1 queries: loading 50 posts then querying the author for each → batch (`WHERE id IN`) or join; DataLoader pattern in GraphQL.
Long transactions hold locks and block vacuum; keep transactions short, never wait on network calls inside them.
Pagination: keyset (`WHERE created_at < ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`) beats OFFSET for deep pages.

items.q: SQL or NoSQL for an order system?
items.a: SQL: orders need transactions across order, items, payment status; scale with read replicas and shard by customer_id when needed.

items.q: Why is my query slow even with an index?
items.a: Wrong column order, function on the column, low selectivity, stale stats, or the planner chose a scan; check EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

items.q: How do you add a column to a 2 billion row table safely?
items.a: Online schema change (gh-ost/pt-online-schema-change, or Postgres ADD COLUMN with default is metadata-only in v11+), expand-contract migrations.

items.q: Wide-column partition is growing forever. Fix?
items.a: Add a time bucket to the partition key and query across buckets.

topics.title: Replication
topics.summary: Copies for availability and read scale; leader-follower, multi-leader or leaderless, each with its own lag and conflict story.

blocks.caption: Single-leader: writes to one node, streamed to followers

head: Topology
Strength
Weakness
rows: Leader is write bottleneck; replica lag
Quorums W + R > N; read repair; sloppy quorum

items: **Synchronous**: leader waits for follower ack. No data loss, higher latency, a slow follower blocks writes.
**Asynchronous**: faster, but failover can lose recent writes.
**Semi-sync**: wait for one follower, rest async. Common production compromise.

head: Anomaly
Fix
rows: User doesn't see their own write
Read-your-writes: read from leader for ~N s after a write, or track the write's log position
Data appears then disappears on refresh
Monotonic reads: pin user to one replica
Consistent prefix: keep causally related writes in one partition

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Failover can produce split brain: two leaders accepting writes. Use fencing and a consensus-based election.

head: Method
Ships
Notes
rows: Exact copy; same DB version required (Postgres streaming)

items: Replica lag = how far the follower's applied position trails the leader's; monitor in seconds and bytes.
Failover: detect leader failure (heartbeats), elect the most up-to-date follower, repoint clients, fence the old leader.
N replicas; write to W, read from R. If W + R > N, read and write sets overlap → at least one replica has the latest value.
N=3, W=2, R=2: tolerates 1 failure for both reads and writes.
**Read repair:** reader notices a stale replica and fixes it. **Anti-entropy:** background Merkle-tree comparison.
**Hinted handoff / sloppy quorum:** another node accepts writes for a down node and hands them back later — more available, weaker guarantee.
Conflicts from concurrent writes: last-write-wins (lossy), vector clocks + app merge, or CRDTs.

head: Strategy
How
Risk
rows: Each record writable in one region
Data types that merge (counters, sets, sequences)

items: Async cross-region replication: RPO = replication lag (seconds); sync cross-region adds 50–200 ms per write.
Read-local / write-home: route writes to the record's home region, read from local replica, use read-your-writes tokens.
Global databases (Spanner, CockroachDB, Aurora Global, DynamoDB Global Tables) package these trade-offs.

items.q: User updates profile then refreshes and sees the old one. Why and fix?
items.a: Read went to a lagging replica. Read from the leader for that user for a short window, or pass the write's LSN and wait for a replica that has it.

items.q: What's split brain and how do you prevent it?
items.a: Two nodes both accept writes as leader. Use consensus-based election with a majority and fence the old leader (STONITH, fencing tokens, revoking its lease).

items.q: Sync or async replication for payments?
items.a: Synchronous (or semi-sync to at least one replica / quorum commit) so an acknowledged payment survives leader loss.

topics.title: Sharding & Consistent Hashing
topics.summary: Partition data when one node can't take the writes or hold the data; the shard key decides everything.

items: High cardinality and even distribution of **both** reads and writes.
Matches the hottest query so it hits one shard.
Examples: messages by channel_id, orders by customer_id, URLs by short code.

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Sharding by created_at sends all new writes to one shard. Sharding by country puts India on one overloaded node.

items: Nodes and keys hash onto a ring (0 … 2^32). A key belongs to the next node clockwise.
Adding/removing a node only moves keys in one arc, ~1/N of data.
**Virtual nodes** (100–200 per server) even out load and allow weighted capacity.
Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, Memcached clients, CDN routing.

head: Problem
Answer
rows: Denormalize or join in the app
Scatter-gather, or a separate index table keyed by the attribute
Split key with random suffix, cache in front
Pre-split into many logical shards mapped to fewer physical nodes

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'll shard by channel_id so one channel's messages live together, and pre-split into 1,024 logical shards so we can rebalance without rehashing.

items: **Fixed many partitions:** create 1,024–4,096 logical shards upfront; move whole shards between nodes (Elasticsearch, Couchbase, Vitess keyspace ranges).
**Dynamic splitting:** split a range when it grows past a size (HBase, DynamoDB, CockroachDB).
**Consistent hashing with vnodes:** adding a node steals small ranges from many nodes.
Move data online: dual-write or stream changes, backfill, verify, cut over routing, delete old copy.

items.title: Backfill
items.text: Copy the shard snapshot to the new node.

items.title: Cut over
items.text: Briefly pause writes or use routing version, switch the directory.

items.title: Clean up
items.text: Delete the old copy after verification.

head: Approach
Example
rows: Cassandra drivers know the token ring

items: **Ring + virtual nodes:** classic; O(log V) lookup with sorted tokens.
**Rendezvous (HRW) hashing:** score = hash(key, node) for every node, pick max — no ring, minimal movement, O(N) per lookup.
**Jump consistent hash:** tiny, fast, perfect balance, but nodes only appended/removed at the end.
**Bounded-load consistent hashing:** cap each node at (1+ε)× average to stop hot spots (used by Vimeo, Google).
**Maglev:** lookup table for LBs with fast lookup and minimal disruption.
Secondary-index lookups: local indexes (query every shard — scatter-gather) vs global index table partitioned by the indexed column (extra write).
Aggregates: compute per shard, merge centrally; or stream to an OLAP store.
Global unique constraint (username): a separate table sharded by username, written with the user record in a saga or 2PC.
IDs that embed the shard (Instagram's ID: time + shard id + sequence) route lookups without a directory.

items.q: When do you shard?
items.a: When a single primary can't handle write throughput or the data no longer fits (after vertical scaling, read replicas and caching).

items.q: Pick a shard key for a multi-tenant SaaS.
items.a: tenant_id keeps tenant data together and isolated; split very large tenants across multiple shards (tenant_id + sub-key).

items.q: Resharding from 8 to 16 with mod N?
items.a: Almost all keys move. Instead pre-split into many logical shards or use consistent hashing; migrate with dual writes and backfill.

topics.title: Storage Engines: B-Trees, LSM & Columnar
topics.summary: Why Postgres, Cassandra and ClickHouse behave so differently: B-tree vs LSM-tree write paths, write-ahead logs, compaction, and row vs column layouts for OLTP vs analytics.

blocks.text: Every serious database appends a change to a sequential log and fsyncs it before acknowledging the write, then updates data structures lazily. After a crash, replay the log. The WAL is also what replication ships to followers.

cols.title: B-tree (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB)
pros: Reads: O(log n) page lookups, predictable
Good for read-heavy OLTP and range scans
cons: Random in-place page writes; write amplification from page splits

cols.title: LSM-tree (Cassandra, RocksDB, DynamoDB storage)
pros: Writes: append to memtable + log — very fast, sequential
cons: Reads may check several SSTables (Bloom filters help)

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Write-heavy, append-mostly data (events, messages, metrics) points to an LSM engine; read-heavy relational data with transactions points to a B-tree engine.

items.title: Flush
items.text: When full, write an immutable sorted SSTable.

items.title: Compaction
items.text: Merge SSTables, drop overwritten values and expired tombstones (size-tiered vs leveled).

cols.title: Row store (OLTP)
cons: Scanning one column across a billion rows reads everything

cols.title: Column store (OLAP: ClickHouse, BigQuery, Parquet)
pros: Read only the columns a query needs

blocks.text: Typical architecture: OLTP database for the product, CDC into a columnar warehouse for analytics.

items.q: Why are LSM deletes tricky?
items.a: A delete is a tombstone; until compaction removes older versions everywhere, the tombstone must persist or data resurrects.

items.q: What is a covering index?
items.a: An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself isn't read.

items.q: Why is Parquet used in data lakes?
items.a: Columnar, compressed, splittable files with schema — cheap scans of a few columns.

topics.title: CAP, PACELC & Consistency
topics.summary: Decide per piece of data how stale it may be; say CP or AP with a concrete reason.

blocks.text: During a network **partition** a system chooses **consistency** (reject or block some requests) or **availability** (answer, maybe stale). PACELC adds: **else**, choose **latency** or **consistency**.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: For the ledger I choose CP: I'd rather reject a transfer than double-spend. For like counts, AP: a few seconds stale is fine.

head: Model
Guarantee
Example
rows: Reads see the latest write, real-time order

items: CAP's C is **linearizability**, A means every non-failing node answers; P (partitions) will happen, so the real choice is during a partition.
Most systems aren't purely CP or AP: they choose per operation (DynamoDB strongly consistent reads vs eventual reads; Cassandra QUORUM vs ONE).
PACELC is more useful day to day: even without partitions, strong consistency costs latency (cross-AZ round trips).

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Choose consistency per data type and per operation, not per system.

head: Guarantee
Means
How to provide
rows: Read from leader / sticky replica / wait for LSN
A reply is ordered after what you read

cols.title: Linearizability
pros: Single-object recency: behaves like one copy in real time
cons: Needs consensus or single leader; cross-region latency

cols.title: Serializability
pros: Multi-object transactions behave as if run one by one

blocks.text: Strict serializability = both (Spanner). In interviews: 'linearizable' for a lock or a counter you read immediately; 'serializable' for transaction isolation.

items: Make operations commutative/idempotent so order doesn't matter (counters, sets, CRDTs).
Show pending states in the UI (optimistic updates with reconciliation).
Use compensations instead of rollbacks (sagas).
Monitor and bound staleness (replication lag SLO).

items.q: Is DynamoDB CP or AP?
items.a: Configurable per read: eventually consistent reads (AP-ish, cheaper) or strongly consistent reads from the leader replica; global tables are multi-region last-writer-wins.

items.q: Where do you need strong consistency in an e-commerce site?
items.a: Payments, inventory decrement for the last items, order state transitions, unique coupon redemption.

items.q: How would you build a 'likes' counter?
items.a: Eventually consistent: increment in a sharded counter or via event aggregation; exact count not needed instantly.

topics.title: Transactions & Locks
topics.summary: Isolation levels, optimistic vs pessimistic locking, and distributed locks with fencing tokens.

blocks.text: **MVCC** gives each transaction a snapshot so readers never block writers. **Write skew**: two doctors each check 'someone else is on call' and both go off call. Only serializable or explicit locks stop it.

cols.title: Pessimistic
pros: Right for high contention (last seat, hot inventory)
cons: Deadlock risk: lock in a fixed order, set timeouts

blocks.caption: Lock + fencing token = safe for correctness

items: **Redis**: `SET lock:x <uuid> NX PX 30000`; release with Lua compare-and-delete. Fast, fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work).
**The failure**: a GC pause outlives the TTL; two holders act at once.
**Fencing token**: lock grants an increasing number; storage rejects writes with an older token.
**Correctness locks**: etcd leases or ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znodes (built on consensus).
**DB-native**: unique constraints, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` job queues, advisory locks.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: A Redis lock is fine to avoid duplicate work. If correctness depends on it, I'd add fencing tokens or use etcd.

head: Approach
How
Trade-off
rows: Atomic but blocking if coordinator dies
Common in payments; more API surface

head: Anomaly
Example
Prevented by
rows: Read uncommitted value that rolls back
Same row read twice, different values
Range query returns new rows the second time
Atomic ops, SELECT FOR UPDATE, optimistic versions
Two doctors both go off call
Serializable, or lock the rows you check (FOR UPDATE)

items: **2PL (two-phase locking):** shared/exclusive locks held to commit; serializable but blocks and deadlocks.
**MVCC snapshot isolation:** readers don't block writers; first-committer-wins on write conflicts.
**SSI (serializable snapshot isolation, Postgres SERIALIZABLE):** tracks read/write dependencies and aborts dangerous ones; retry on serialization failure.
**Next-key / gap locks (InnoDB):** lock index ranges to prevent phantoms in REPEATABLE READ.
Deadlock: T1 holds A wants B, T2 holds B wants A. DB detects the cycle and aborts one — the app must retry.
Prevent: lock in a consistent order (sort IDs), keep transactions short, use lock timeouts.
Hot rows (one inventory row for a flash sale) serialize all buyers: split the counter (N sub-rows), or move the counter to Redis with an async ledger.
`SKIP LOCKED` turns a table into a job queue: workers grab unlocked rows without waiting.

head: Option
Correct under pauses?
Notes
rows: Simple if you already have the DB

blocks.text:
Fencing:
 lock service grants token 33 to A; A pauses (GC); lease expires
 B gets token 34 and writes with 34; storage remembers max=34
 A wakes, writes with 33 → storage rejects (33 < 34)

items: **2PC:** prepare (participants vote and hold locks) → commit/abort. Blocking if coordinator fails after prepare; XA in Java EE; used inside databases (Spanner uses 2PC over Paxos groups).
**Saga:** local transactions + compensations; must handle out-of-order and duplicate messages; semantic locks (status = PENDING) prevent dirty reads of in-flight sagas.
**TCC:** Try reserves (hold funds), Confirm commits, Cancel releases; reservations expire.
**Outbox + idempotent consumers:** the practical backbone of sagas.

items.q: Two users book the last seat. Walk through it.
items.a: Seat row `status=FREE`. `UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', user=? , hold_until=now()+10m WHERE id=? AND status='FREE'`; 1 row updated = success, 0 = taken. Payment then confirms; expired holds are released by a job.

items.q: Optimistic or pessimistic for a wiki?
items.a: Optimistic with version numbers; conflicts are rare and you can show a merge screen.

items.q: Why not just use a Redis lock for payments?
items.a: A lock can expire while the holder still runs; use DB transactions/constraints and idempotency keys; if a lock is used, add fencing tokens.

topics.title: Consensus & Leader Election
topics.summary: Raft and Paxos let a majority agree on one ordered log; the basis of etcd, ZooKeeper and Kafka KRaft.

items: Nodes are follower, candidate or leader; a follower that hears no heartbeat times out (randomized) and runs for leader.
A candidate wins with votes from a majority for that term.
The leader appends client commands to its log and replicates them.
An entry is committed once a majority stores it; then it is applied.
Tolerates ⌊(N−1)/2⌋ failures: 3 nodes survive 1, 5 survive 2.

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Even node counts add no fault tolerance: 4 nodes still survive only 1 failure. Use 3 or 5.

Wall clocks drift, so never order events across machines by timestamp alone. **Lamport clocks** give a causal total order, **vector clocks** detect concurrent writes, **hybrid logical clocks** mix both, and Spanner's **TrueTime** waits out clock uncertainty.

items: **Terms:** logical clock; each election starts a new term; stale leaders step down when they see a higher term.
**Election:** follower times out (150–300 ms randomized), becomes candidate, votes for itself, requests votes; a node votes once per term and only for candidates whose log is at least as up to date.
**Log replication:** leader appends entry, sends AppendEntries; once a majority store it, it's committed and applied to the state machine.
**Log matching:** each entry carries (term, index); followers reject mismatches and the leader backs up until logs agree.
**Safety:** a committed entry is in every future leader's log (election restriction).
**Snapshots** compact the log; **membership changes** via joint consensus or one-at-a-time.

blocks.caption: Writes go through the leader to a majority

head: Protocol
Used by
Note
rows: Proposers, acceptors, learners; leader optimisation = Multi-Paxos
etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, Kafka KRaft

items: Leader election (one scheduler, one primary DB).
Distributed locks and leases with fencing.
Configuration and service discovery (etcd, Consul).
Replicated state machines (each Raft group owns a range in CockroachDB/TiKV).
Atomic commit across shards (Spanner: 2PC across Paxos groups).

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Consensus is slow per operation (majority round trip, fsync). Keep it for metadata and coordination, not every user write — unless the database is built on it.
Across 3 AZs, run 3 or 5 nodes so losing an AZ still leaves a majority.

items.q: Why randomized election timeouts?
items.a: To avoid split votes where several candidates start at once and nobody wins.

items.q: Can a Raft leader serve reads locally?
items.a: Only safely if it confirms it's still leader (read index with a heartbeat round, or leader leases with bounded clock drift).

items.q: What happens during a network partition with 5 nodes split 3/2?
items.a: The side with 3 can elect a leader and commit; the 2-node side can't make progress — that's CP behaviour.

topics.title: Quorums, Gossip & Failure Detection
topics.summary: The primitives behind leaderless databases and cluster membership: R + W > N quorums, sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, vector clocks, Merkle-tree anti-entropy, heartbeats, leases and gossip.

head: Config (N=3)
Behaviour
rows: Fastest; no overlap → stale reads possible

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set, so a read sees at least one copy of the latest acknowledged write.

When the key's home replicas are unreachable, accept the write on other nodes with a 'hint' naming the intended owner, and hand it off when the owner returns. This keeps writes available during partitions at the cost of weaker consistency.

cols.title: Last-write-wins (timestamps)
cons: Silently drops concurrent writes; depends on clocks

cols.title: Vector clocks / version vectors
pros: Detect true concurrency; client merges siblings

cols.title: CRDTs
cons: Only for data types that have a CRDT

blocks.text: Each replica builds a hash tree over its key ranges. Two replicas compare root hashes; if they differ, recurse only into differing children. Divergent ranges are found with O(log n) comparisons and only those keys are synced.

items: **Heartbeats:** periodic 'I'm alive' messages; missing k in a row → suspect.
**Gossip:** every second each node exchanges its membership table with a few random peers; information spreads to all nodes in O(log n) rounds — no central coordinator (Cassandra, Consul/Serf).
**Phi-accrual detector:** outputs a suspicion level from inter-arrival times instead of a fixed timeout.
**Leases:** time-bounded ownership (e.g. leader lease). Pair with **fencing tokens** so a paused old owner can't corrupt state.

items.q: Why add fencing tokens to a lease?
items.a: A GC pause can outlive the lease; storage rejects writes with a token older than the latest one issued.

items.q: Is a quorum system linearizable?
items.a: Not automatically — concurrent writes, sloppy quorums and LWW clocks break it; linearizability needs consensus or read-repair with extra rules.

items.q: How fast does gossip converge?
items.a: Roughly log_fanout(N) rounds — a 1,000-node cluster in a handful of seconds.

topics.title: Queues & Kafka
topics.summary: Decouple with queues for jobs and logs for events; know partitions, consumer groups, ISR and delivery semantics.

blocks.caption: One consumer per partition inside a group

items: Partition = ordered, append-only log; hash(key) keeps one entity's events in order.
Replication factor 3, `acks=all`, `min.insync.replicas=2` → no loss on one broker failure.
ISR = replicas caught up with the leader; only they can become leader.
Max consumer parallelism = number of partitions.
Fast because of sequential I/O, page cache, zero-copy, batching, compression.
Log compaction keeps the latest value per key.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'll use at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers keyed by event ID; that's exactly-once in effect.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Failed N times? Send to a dead letter queue and alert on its depth. One poison message must not block a partition.

sections.title: Visibility timeouts, acks and poison messages

items: SQS: a received message is hidden for the visibility timeout; if not deleted it reappears → set timeout > processing time, extend for long jobs.
RabbitMQ: unacked messages are redelivered when the consumer dies; `prefetch` bounds in-flight messages per consumer.
Kafka: committing the offset is the ack; a consumer crash before commit reprocesses from the last commit.
Poison messages: count deliveries (`ApproximateReceiveCount`, x-death headers) and route to a DLQ after N attempts.
Retry topics with increasing delays (retry-1m, retry-10m) avoid blocking the main partition.
Global order requires a single partition (throughput ceiling). Usually you need order **per entity**: key by entity ID.
Producer retries can reorder unless idempotence is on (`enable.idempotence=true`, max.in.flight ≤ 5).
Rebalances can cause duplicates; consumers dedupe by event ID or idempotent writes.
Processing in parallel inside a consumer breaks per-key order unless you parallelize by key.
Partitions = max consumer parallelism. Size for peak: e.g. 200 MB/s ÷ 10 MB/s per consumer = 20 partitions, round up to 32–64.
Adding partitions later remaps keys → order breaks for in-flight keys; plan ahead.
Skewed keys create hot partitions; salt very hot keys or use a sub-key.
Consumer lag (latest offset − committed offset) is the key health metric; alert on lag growth and time-lag.
Kafka Streams / Flink: stateful processing with local state stores backed by changelog topics.
Windows: tumbling (fixed), hopping (overlapping), sliding, session (gap-based).
Event time vs processing time; watermarks decide when a window is complete; late events go to side outputs.
Exactly-once in Flink via checkpoints (Chandy-Lamport) + transactional sinks.

items.q: Why add a queue between an API and a slow service?
items.a: Absorbs spikes, decouples availability, enables retries and back-pressure; the API returns 202 Accepted with a job ID.

items.q: How do you guarantee order and scale?
items.a: Partition by the key that needs order; parallelism across keys; one consumer per partition.

items.q: A consumer is 2 hours behind. What do you do?
items.a: Scale consumers up to the partition count, optimize per-message work (batching), check for a poison message or hot partition, temporarily skip non-critical work.

items.q: Kafka or SQS for sending emails?
items.a: SQS (or RabbitMQ): simple work queue, per-message visibility and DLQ; Kafka is overkill unless you also need replay/many consumers.

topics.title: Outbox, Saga & CQRS
topics.summary: Patterns that keep services consistent without distributed transactions.

blocks.caption: Dual-write solved: one DB transaction, relay publishes

blocks.text: Writing to the DB and to Kafka separately can fail half-way. Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it (at-least-once).

head: Style
Pro
Con
rows: Flow is hard to see and debug
Orchestrator is a component to run

items: **CQRS**: write model (validated, normalized) separate from read models (denormalized per screen), synced by events.
**Event sourcing**: the event log is the truth; state = replay + snapshots. Audit trail for free; schema evolution is harder.
Natural fit: ledgers, trading, order lifecycles.
Delivery is at-least-once; consumers dedupe by event ID (inbox table).
Keep per-aggregate order by keying Kafka messages by aggregate_id.
Clean up sent rows or partition the outbox table by day.

head: Concern
Answer
rows: No global isolation; use semantic locks (status PENDING) and commutative updates
Business undo (refund, release stock), not a DB rollback; must be idempotent
Step after which the saga only goes forward (e.g. payment captured)
Saga ID propagated through every event; state table per saga

items: State = fold(events). Commands are validated against current state, then emit events appended to the aggregate's stream with optimistic concurrency (expected version).
Snapshots every N events speed up loading.
Projections build read models; rebuild by replaying from offset 0.
Schema evolution: upcasters convert old event versions; never edit past events.
GDPR: crypto-shredding (encrypt personal data per user, delete the key).

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Event sourcing everywhere is over-engineering. Use it where history is the product: ledgers, trading, audit-heavy workflows.

head: Pattern
What
When
rows: Route slices of a monolith to new services gradually
Proxy next to each service for mTLS, retries, metrics
Dedupe table of processed message IDs

items.q: Choreography or orchestration?
items.a: Choreography for 2–3 simple steps; orchestration once there are many steps, timeouts, or you need to see and debug the flow.

items.q: How do you avoid the dual-write problem?
items.a: Transactional outbox or CDC; never write DB then publish in two separate calls without one.

items.q: How do CQRS read models stay consistent?
items.a: Eventually: projections consume events; return the write's version so clients can wait or show pending state.

topics.title: Stream Processing & Change Data Capture
topics.summary: Process events continuously: event time vs processing time, windows and watermarks, stateful operators with checkpoints, exactly-once sinks, and CDC to stream a database's changes into everything else.

cols.title: Batch (Spark, MapReduce)
pros: Great for daily reports, ML training

cols.title: Stream (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming)
cons: State, ordering and late data to manage

items: **Event time** = when it happened; **processing time** = when you saw it. Aggregate on event time for correct results.
**Windows:** tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping), session (gap-based).
**Watermark:** an assertion that no events older than T will arrive; a window closes when the watermark passes its end. Late events go to a side output or update results.
Operators keep keyed state (counts, joins) locally (RocksDB), checkpointed periodically to durable storage together with source offsets.
On failure, restore the last checkpoint and replay from those offsets → **exactly-once state**.
**Exactly-once output** needs transactional sinks (two-phase commit) or idempotent upserts keyed deterministically.

blocks.text: CDC tails a database's replication log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) and publishes each row change as an event (Debezium → Kafka). It keeps search indexes, caches, warehouses and other services in sync without dual writes from the application.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Dual writes (write DB, then publish to Kafka in app code). One of the two can fail, leaving them inconsistent. Use CDC or the transactional outbox.

cols.title: Lambda
pros: Batch layer is authoritative; stream gives fast approximations

cols.title: Kappa
pros: Single streaming path; reprocess by replaying the log
cons: Needs long log retention and replay capacity

items.q: What is backpressure?
items.a: When a downstream operator is slow, upstream slows down instead of buffering unboundedly; Flink does it via credit-based flow control.

items.q: How do you join two streams?
items.a: Windowed join on a key, holding each side's events in state for the window duration.

items.q: Why partition by key?
items.a: All events for a key go to one operator instance, so its state is local and ordering per key is preserved.

topics.title: Workflows & Long-Running Jobs
topics.summary: Coordinate multi-step processes that take seconds to days: job queues with retries, durable workflow engines (Temporal, Step Functions), sagas with compensation, timers and human-in-the-loop steps.

sections.title: When you need more than a queue

items: A single async task (resize an image) → a job queue + workers.
Several dependent steps with retries, timeouts and branching (order → payment → inventory → shipping) → a **workflow**.
Steps that wait hours or days (approval, trial expiry) → durable timers.

blocks.text: Workflow engines persist every step's result in an event history. If a worker crashes mid-workflow, another worker replays the history to rebuild state and continues from the next step. The workflow code looks sequential, but each step (an 'activity') is retried independently with its own timeout.

cols.title: Temporal / Cadence
pros: Workflow as code; long-running; strong replay semantics

items.title: On failure
items.text: Run compensations in reverse order for completed steps.

items: Return 202 + a job id immediately; clients poll status or receive a webhook/SSE event.
Every step idempotent (step id as idempotency key) because retries are guaranteed.
Heartbeats for long activities so stuck workers are detected.
Store large intermediate data in blob storage and pass references.

items.q: Why must Temporal workflow code be deterministic?
items.a: Recovery replays the code against recorded history; non-deterministic calls (random, time, I/O) would diverge — they belong in activities.

items.q: Saga vs 2PC?
items.a: 2PC locks resources across services and blocks on coordinator failure; sagas commit locally and compensate, trading isolation for availability.

items.q: How do you show progress for a 20-minute job?
items.a: Workers update a progress record; the client subscribes via SSE or polls the job status endpoint.

topics.title: Rate Limiting
topics.summary: Token bucket for bursty APIs, sliding windows for accuracy, Redis + Lua for distributed counters.

blocks.text:
-- token bucket: KEYS[1]=bucket, ARGV = capacity, rate/s, now
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (ARGV[3] - ts) * ARGV[2])
local ok = tokens >= 1
if ok then tokens = tokens - 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60)
return ok and 1 or 0

items: Key by user, API key, IP or tenant tier: `rl:{user}:{endpoint}`.
Return **429** with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining.
Decide **fail-open** vs **fail-closed** if Redis is down.
For extreme scale, keep local counters and sync to Redis periodically (approximate).
**Token bucket:** tokens = min(cap, tokens + (now − last) × rate); allow if tokens ≥ 1. Parameters: rate (average) and capacity (burst).
**Leaky bucket (queue):** requests enter a FIFO drained at a constant rate; overflow rejected. Smooths output.
**Fixed window:** count per window key `rl:u:minute`; boundary burst up to 2× limit.
**Sliding log:** store each timestamp in a sorted set; exact; memory O(requests).
**Sliding window counter:** estimate = current_count + previous_count × (1 − elapsed/window); ~accurate with 2 counters.
**GCRA** (generic cell rate algorithm): token bucket expressed as a single 'theoretical arrival time' value — one key, used by redis-cell.

blocks.text:
Sliding window counter example: limit 100/min
 previous minute = 80, current = 30, 25% into current minute
 estimate = 30 + 80 × 0.75 = 90 → allow

head: Approach
Accuracy
Latency
Notes
rows: Lua for atomicity; Redis becomes critical path
Each node gets a share of the quota
Hash clients to one limiter node

items: Dimensions: per user, API key, IP, endpoint, tenant tier; global limits protect shared backends.
Respond 429 with `Retry-After`, `RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` headers.
Different limits for reads vs writes; cost-based limits (tokens for LLM APIs, query cost for GraphQL).
Fail-open for availability (most APIs) vs fail-closed for abuse-sensitive endpoints (login, OTP).
Layered: edge/WAF for DDoS, gateway for per-client quotas, service-level concurrency limits.
Concurrency limits (Netflix concurrency-limits, TCP-Vegas-style) adjust allowed in-flight requests based on latency.
Priority shedding: drop background and free-tier traffic first.
Queue with deadline: drop requests that would time out anyway.

items.q: Design a rate limiter for a public API.
items.a: Token bucket per API key in Redis via Lua at the gateway; config per plan; 429 + headers; local fallback limits if Redis is down; metrics on rejections.

items.q: Login brute-force protection?
items.a: Limit per account and per IP with exponential lockout, CAPTCHA after N failures, fail-closed.

items.q: Why not fixed windows?
items.a: Burst of 2× at boundaries; use sliding window counter for nearly the same cost.

topics.title: Idempotency, Retries & Circuit Breakers
topics.summary: Assume calls fail, are slow, or arrive twice; contain the blast radius.

blocks.caption: Repeat key returns the stored response

items: Client makes one UUID per logical operation and reuses it on retry.
Server inserts key as IN_PROGRESS (unique constraint); duplicates wait or get 409.
On finish store the response for ~24 h; a retry gets the same response, no second charge.
Every call has a timeout shorter than its caller's.
Exponential backoff with **full jitter**: sleep = random(0, base × 2^n), capped.
Retry budget ≈ 10% of traffic; retry only idempotent calls on transient errors.

items.title: Open
items.text: Threshold crossed (e.g. 50% in 10 s): fail fast, use fallback.

items.title: Half-open
items.text: After cool-down let a few probes through; success closes, failure reopens.

items: **Bulkhead**: separate pools per dependency.
**Load shedding**: drop low-priority work first.
**Graceful degradation**: stale cache, hide widgets, read-only mode.
SLI → SLO → SLA; RPO (data loss allowed) and RTO (recovery time) drive DR design.
Set connect and request timeouts on every call; defaults are often infinite.
Propagate deadlines (gRPC deadline, header) so downstream services stop work the caller abandoned.
Timeout budget: caller 1 s → service A 800 ms → its call to B 300 ms.
Hedged requests: after p95 latency, send a duplicate to another replica and take the first response (idempotent reads only).

sections.title: Retries that don't make things worse

blocks.text:
sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))      # full jitter
retry only on: timeouts, 429, 502, 503, 504, connection reset
never retry: 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 (business errors)
retry budget: retries ≤ 10% of requests per client

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Retries at every layer multiply: 3 layers × 3 retries = 27 calls to the bottom service during an outage. Retry at one layer only.

head: Parameter
Typical
rows: 50% over a sliding window of 20–100 calls

blocks.text: Pair with fallbacks: cached data, default, queued for later, or a clear error. Breakers per dependency (and per host for outlier ejection).

items: Idempotency key table: `(key PK, request_hash, status, response, created_at)` with a unique constraint.
Same key + different payload → 422 (client bug).
Naturally idempotent operations: PUT full resource, `SET status='PAID' WHERE status='PENDING'`.
Consumers: dedupe by message ID (inbox) or make writes upserts.
Expire keys after the retry window (24 h–7 d).
Chaos engineering: kill instances, inject latency, partition networks in staging and (carefully) production.
Game days for failover drills; measure RTO/RPO for real.
Load tests at 2× expected peak; soak tests for leaks.

items.q: Payment API timed out. Did it charge?
items.a: Unknown — so retry with the same idempotency key; the server returns the original result if it already processed it.

items.q: What's a retry storm and how do you stop it?
items.a: Synchronized retries amplifying an outage; jittered exponential backoff, retry budgets, circuit breakers, and server-side load shedding.

items.q: Liveness vs readiness probes?
items.a: Liveness failing restarts the container; readiness failing removes it from load balancing without restart (e.g. while warming caches).

items: gRPC: Protobuf schemas, HTTP/2 multiplexing, unary + server/client/bidi streaming, deadlines, generated clients. Needs gRPC-Web or a gateway for browsers.

GraphQL: single endpoint, typed schema, client picks fields; solve N+1 with DataLoader batching; protect with depth/complexity limits and persisted queries; caching via normalized client caches (Apollo) since HTTP caching is harder.
Federation (Apollo) composes subgraphs owned by different teams.
**Long polling:** server holds the request until data or ~30 s timeout; client re-requests immediately.
**SSE:** `Content-Type: text/event-stream`; `id:` lets the browser resume with `Last-Event-ID`; HTTP/1.1 browsers limit ~6 connections per domain (fine on HTTP/2).
**WebSocket:** HTTP `Upgrade` → full-duplex frames; needs ping/pong heartbeats, auth on connect (token in first message or cookie), and reconnect logic.
**WebRTC:** peer-to-peer UDP with ICE/STUN/TURN; SFU servers for group calls.
**MQTT:** lightweight pub/sub for IoT over TCP, QoS levels 0/1/2.
Connection tier (gateways) is stateful; business tier stateless.
Presence/registry store: user → gateway ID with TTL refreshed by heartbeat.
Message routing: pub/sub channel per gateway or per topic (Redis, NATS, Kafka for durable).
Delivery guarantees: sequence numbers per conversation; client acks; resend gap on reconnect.
Backpressure: drop or coalesce updates for slow clients (latest-value-wins for presence, prices).

items.q: How do you authenticate a WebSocket?
items.a: Short-lived token from the HTTP API passed on connect (query param over TLS or first message); gateway validates and binds user ID to the socket; re-auth on expiry.

items.q: SSE or WebSocket for live sports scores?
items.a: SSE: one-way, simple, works through proxies and auto-reconnects.

items.q: How do you scale to 10M WebSocket connections?
items.a: ~200 gateways at 50k each, L4 LB, connection registry, pub/sub routing, jittered reconnects, heartbeats; tune kernel (file descriptors, memory per socket).

Split along business capabilities with their own data; never share a database between services.
Distributed transactions across services → sagas, not 2PC.

items.q: How do you avoid cascading failures?
items.a: Timeouts on every call, retries with budgets and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallbacks.

items.q: How do you trace a request across 10 services?
items.a: Propagate a trace id (W3C traceparent) and emit spans to a tracing backend (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/Tempo).

items.q: What does the gateway do for auth?
items.a: Validates the token (JWT/OAuth) and passes identity claims downstream; services still authorise actions.

Durability: 3× replication or erasure coding (10+4 survives 4 losses at 1.4× cost).
Lifecycle rules tier cold data to cheaper storage.

Image resizing on the fly at the edge or pre-generated variants.

Content-addressed storage (hash as key) gives dedup for free.

items.q: Where do you store image metadata?

items.q: How do you prevent hotlinking of private files?
items.a: Private bucket + short-lived signed URLs (or signed cookies at the CDN).

items: Bit array of m bits + k hash functions. Insert: set k bits. Query: if any bit is 0 → **definitely not present**; if all are 1 → **probably present**.
No false negatives; false-positive rate p ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k. About **9.6 bits per element for 1% FP**, ~14.4 bits for 0.1%.
Can't delete (use a counting Bloom filter or Cuckoo filter).

head: Used for
Why

blocks.text: Estimates the number of distinct elements using ~12 KB per counter (Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT) with ~0.8% standard error, for any cardinality. Hash each element, use the first bits to pick a register, and record the longest run of leading zeros. HLLs **merge** by taking the max per register — perfect for daily-unique-users rolled up into monthly.

items: A d × w table of counters with d hash functions. Increment one counter per row; estimate = min over rows.
Overestimates (collisions) but never underestimates; error ≈ total/w with probability 1 − e^(−d).
Combine with a min-heap of size K to track **top-K heavy hitters** in a stream.

items.q: How do you enforce document permissions in RAG?
